en: A state of temporary suspension or inactivity
hook: ABEYANCE: 'A BAY' where ships wait, temporarily paused.
story: When the funding ran out, plans for the new bridge were held in abeyance; nothing was cancelled, but nothing moved either. Abeyance means temporary suspension. A law in abeyance is not currently enforced.

en: Existing as an idea rather than a physical thing; not concrete
hook: ABSTRACT: pulled away (abs-tract) from the physical world.
story: Love, freedom, and justice are abstract ideas; you can't touch them. Math can feel abstract until a teacher connects it to real life, like calculating bus fare. Abstract means conceptual, not concrete. Abstract art doesn't represent real objects.

en: An open insult; to insult intentionally
hook: AFFRONT: an insult right to your FRONT, to your face.
story: Not inviting the groom's uncle to the wedding was seen as an affront to the whole family; it sparked a feud for years. An affront is a public insult. Corruption is an affront to honest taxpayers.

en: To make someone troubled or nervous; to campaign to arouse public concern
hook: AGITATE: like a washing machine's AGITATOR, stirring things up.
story: News of the price hike agitated the workers, who began agitating for higher wages with marches and strikes. To agitate is to disturb someone emotionally, or to campaign for change. A washing machine agitates clothes.

en: Respected and impressive; majestic
hook: GRE trick: au-GUST, like Emperor AUGUSTUS, majestic.
story: The young researcher felt nervous presenting before such an august audience: Nobel laureates, university presidents, and famous scientists. August, pronounced aw-GUST, means respected and impressive. Named after the Roman emperor Augustus.

en: To polish until shiny; to enhance a reputation
hook: BURNISH: rub until it BURNS bright.
story: The silversmith burnished the old tray until it shone like new. Before the election, the candidate tried to burnish his image by donating to schools and posing with farmers. To burnish is to polish or to improve a reputation.

en: Pretending to be shy; reluctant to give details
hook: COY: playing it COOL and shy.
story: When asked about her new boyfriend, Nadia was coy: 'Maybe, maybe not,' she said with a smile. The company was coy about its profits, refusing to give numbers. Coy means pretending to be shy, or deliberately evasive about information.

en: To express disapproval of; to belittle
hook: DEPRECATE: like DEPRECIATE, lowering something's value.
story: The teacher deprecated the practice of copying homework, calling it self-defeating. Self-deprecating humor makes fun of yourself: 'I'm so bad at math, I count on my fingers.' To deprecate is to express disapproval or belittle.

en: The feeling that something is unworthy of respect; to scorn
hook: DIS-DAIN: you won't DEIGN to look at it.
story: The rich students treated the scholarship kids with disdain, sneering at their old shoes and secondhand books. Disdain means contempt, considering someone unworthy. Synonyms: scorn, contempt, derision.

en: To scatter or spread over a wide area
hook: DIS-PERSE: like a SPRAY spreading out.
story: When the rain began, the crowd in the park quickly dispersed, running in every direction to find shelter. Police dispersed the protesters with water cannons. To disperse is to scatter widely. Synonyms: dissipate, scatter.

en: To swell out from internal pressure
hook: DIS-TEND: EXTEND outward, swelling.
story: After eating three plates of biryani at the wedding, Rafi's belly was distended, round and swollen. Malnourished children often have distended stomachs. To distend is to swell from pressure inside.

en: Native to or regularly found in a particular place or group
hook: EN-DEMIC: IN the people (demos), always present there.
story: Malaria is endemic in parts of the Chittagong Hill Tracts; cases appear there every year. Unfortunately, corruption is endemic in some government offices too, deeply rooted and always present. Endemic means native to or regularly found in a particular place. An epidemic is a sudden outbreak; an endemic disease is constantly present.

en: Deep hostility; the state of being enemies
hook: ENMITY: ENEMY-ity.
story: The enmity between the two zamindar families lasted three generations, starting with a dispute over a pond. Even the grandchildren refused to marry across the families. Enmity is deep hostility. Synonyms: animosity, antagonism.

en: Socially awkward; lacking grace or tact
hook: GAUCHE: French for LEFT, as in left-handed and clumsy.
story: At the formal dinner, Tanvir made a gauche remark about the host's weight and then spilled soup on the tablecloth. Gauche means socially awkward and tactless. Its opposite is adroit, from the French for right.

en: Showing uncontrolled emotion; extremely funny
hook: HYSTERICAL: emotions out of control, crying or laughing.
story: When she saw a cockroach on her arm, Mitu became hysterical, screaming and jumping around. Later, the video of it was hysterical; everyone laughed until they cried. Hysterical means wildly emotional, or informally, very funny.

en: Shamelessly rude and disrespectful
hook: IM-PUDENT: no shame (pudor = shame).
story: When the teacher asked him to sit down, the impudent boy replied, 'Make me.' The class went silent. Impudent means boldly disrespectful. Synonyms: insolent, impertinent, brazen.

en: Just begun and not fully formed
hook: INCHOATE: like a chick just INCHing out of its egg, not yet formed.
story: Arif's business idea was still inchoate: a vague notion about helping farmers sell online, with no plan, no budget, and no team. Inchoate means just beginning, not yet fully developed. Synonyms: nascent, incipient, rudimentary.

en: A strong liking or habitual tendency
hook: PENCHANT: leaning toward it like a PENDANT hangs down.
story: Grandpa had a penchant for spicy pickles; he ate them with every meal, even breakfast. Sara has a penchant for detective novels. A penchant is a strong fondness. Synonyms: predilection, propensity.

en: A state of uncertainty over what to do in a difficult situation
hook: QUANDARY: 'QUAND?' (when?) and 'where?' — totally stuck.
story: Nadia was in a quandary: accept the high-paying job in Dhaka, or the scholarship in Germany? Both had deadlines on the same day. A quandary is a difficult choice. Synonyms: dilemma, predicament.

en: Isolation to prevent the spread of disease; to isolate
hook: QUARANTINE: from Italian 'quaranta', forty days of isolation for ships.
story: During the pandemic, travelers arriving in the country were quarantined in hotels for fourteen days. The word comes from the forty days ships once had to wait before docking in Venice. To quarantine is to isolate to prevent spread.

en: To forcefully stop or suppress; to officially reject
hook: QUASH: SQUASH it flat.
story: The government quashed the rumor of a bank collapse with an official statement. The high court quashed the lower court's verdict. To quash is to suppress decisively, or to annul legally.

en: To argue about trivial matters; a minor objection
hook: QUIBBLE: a small QUIBBLE, like a QUIBBLING nibble.
story: The two brothers quibbled for an hour over whose turn it was to take out the trash, while the trash itself sat there. A quibble is a petty argument or minor objection. 'My only quibble with the movie is its length.'

en: To cause severe and extensive damage
hook: RAVAGE: like a RAVENOUS SAVAGE destroying everything.
story: Cyclone Sidr ravaged the southern coast in 2007, destroying homes, crops, and forests across thousands of square kilometers. To ravage is to devastate. Time and disease can also ravage a person's body.

en: To publicly withdraw a statement or belief
hook: RE-CANT: un-CHANT what you said.
story: Galileo was forced to recant his claim that the Earth orbits the sun, saying publicly that he had been wrong. Legend says he whispered, 'And yet it moves.' To recant is to formally take back a statement. Synonyms: retract, abjure.

en: Formidable, especially as an opponent; worthy of respect
hook: RE-DOUBT-ABLE: you DOUBT you can beat them.
story: The chess champion was a redoubtable opponent; nobody had beaten her in five years. Even grandmasters felt nervous facing her. Redoubtable means formidable and inspiring respect or fear. A redoubt was a fortress.

en: Shy and tending to avoid company
hook: GRE trick: RETIRING means shy — she RETIRES to her room when guests come.
story: Mitu's retiring cousin always disappeared into the kitchen when guests arrived and rarely said more than hello. Retiring means shy and reserved, not someone leaving their job. Synonyms: reticent, diffident.

en: High-pitched and piercing; loud and forceful in criticism
hook: SHRILL: like a SHRIEKING whistle.
story: The shrill whistle of the pressure cooker woke the whole house. Critics' shrill attacks on the new policy grew louder each day. Shrill means piercingly high-pitched, or loudly, unpleasantly insistent.

en: Clever but deliberately misleading argument
hook: SOPHISTRY: from the SOPHISTS, Greek teachers who could argue anything.
story: 'If you skip breakfast, you save time; time is money; so skipping meals makes you rich.' That's sophistry: clever-sounding but false reasoning. Sophistry uses tricky logic to deceive. Synonym: specious reasoning.

en: To provide evidence to support or prove
hook: SUBSTANTIATE: give it SUBSTANCE.
story: The journalist couldn't publish the corruption story until she could substantiate it with documents and witnesses. To substantiate is to prove with evidence. Unsubstantiated claims are rumors. Synonyms: corroborate, verify.

en: Skilled at gaining advantage through cunning
hook: WILY: like WILE E. Coyote, always scheming.
story: The wily old shopkeeper always found a way to sell more: free samples, 'last piece' tricks, and compliments that made customers buy things they didn't need. Wily means cleverly cunning. Synonyms: crafty, sly, cunning.
